title: Philidor family: punish the passive rook

difficulty.label: Club player on the strong side of the Philidor who must cash the defender's one passive move

objective.summary: The same Philidor position the defence drill holds — one move after the defender abandoned the third-rank fence for the passive Rh8. The tablebase now says win, and it says something sharper: exactly one move wins it. The defending king stands on its own rook's rank, so the back-rank check is a skewer; every other move on the board — including the natural king-to-the-sixth squeeze — lets the defender re-assemble the draw. Collect the rook, then escort the pawn home with the king in front.

planClasses.label: Check the rank the king blocks
planClasses.description: The passive rook's fatal geometry: its own king stands between it and the checking square, so Ra8+ cannot be met by a capture. The king steps aside and the rook falls. This window is one move wide — the drill's root is the only position in the family where it is open.

planClasses.label: The squeeze that comes too late
planClasses.description: Against passive defence the textbook plan is the king to the sixth and zugzwang — and here the tablebase refutes it: the defender's rook returns to checking and the draw re-assembles. The squeeze is the right plan one family member over; in this position it costs the win.

planClasses.label: Escort: king in front, pawn behind
planClasses.description: Once the rook is won, the conversion is the family's standard escort: the king advances ahead of the pawn and the pawn follows in its shadow. Pushing the pawn first is the concession the defence always waits for.

annotations: The blockade square is taken by your king, not the pawn. The defender's king has only the two back-rank squares, your rook holds the seventh — this is the rook-mate fence from the theoretical-mates drill, arrived at from a real game.
The rook comes back to work: the check clears the king off the seventh rank so the promotion path belongs to White. The pawn itself never needed defending — the rook's rank does the pushing.
Now the pawn steps into the king's shadow — with a tempo. Note the order everywhere in this line: king first, pawn second.
Only now the pawn. It advances into a square its king already guards; nothing to attack, nothing to blockade.
The escort begins: king in front of the pawn. The rook on h8 needs no minding — a bare king can never attack it profitably.
Collect. Rook and pawn against a bare king: the game is decided, and the drill's remaining work is the clean escort.

The skewer. The rook checks along the rank the defending rook needs — and Rxa8 is impossible because the defender's own king blocks the eighth. The king must step off the rank, and h8 falls next move. The tablebase verdict on this position: this is the only winning move.

checkpoints.label: The defender's rook is off the board
The rook-mate fence, reached from a real ending

deviations.note: The textbook squeeze — king to the sixth against a passive rook — queried as a DRAW in this exact position: the rook checks from behind and the defence re-assembles. The shape entry's squeeze plan is real; this is the family member where the skewer preempts it, and hesitating costs the win.

Marching straight ahead — the other natural king move — is also a queried draw: the window closes, the defender lifts the rook off the blocked rank or restores the rear-check machine, and the position returns to the held Philidor of the sibling drill. (The pawn itself cannot even move: its own king stands on e5.)

A waiting move where waiting is the one thing the position does not allow — queried draw. All twenty-one legal White moves at this root were enumerated and queried: Ra8+ wins, thirteen moves draw, and seven moves lose outright because they hang the rook. One move wins; twenty do not.
The only other winning move on the board (queried): the check repeats the question, and after ...Ke8 the skewer stands again. Nothing is lost — and nothing is gained. Rxh8 collects now.

The skewer geometry, turned around: the king has stepped off e8, so the eighth rank now belongs to the defender's rook — Rxb8, and the tablebase calls White LOST. Every quiet rook move along the eighth loses the same way. Verified.

Abandoning the collection for a king move: with e8 vacated the defender simply plays Rxa8 — your rook falls on the same open rank the skewer used. Queried LOSS; all four king moves here lose. The window at this node is one move wide in the other direction.

The rook check works here too — at this node every legal move was queried winning — but it achieves nothing yet: the escort still has to be played. In this pack the checks are saved for the moment the king needs the seventh rank cleared.

STALEMATE, queried as a rules fact — in a rook-up conversion. Ke5 completes a perfect cage by accident: the rook holds the whole eighth rank, the pawn holds d7 and f7, and the king seals the sixth. The winning move Rh7+ clears the seventh instead of sealing the position shut.
Re8+ checks from the square the defending king covers: Kxe8, and the resulting pawn ending was queried a draw. An extra rook is only extra while it is on the board.

feedbackClaims.text: In this exact position the tablebase gives exactly one winning move, Ra8+. All twenty-one legal moves were enumerated and queried: thirteen draw — including the king-to-the-sixth squeeze that is the textbook plan against passive defence — and seven lose by hanging the rook. That exclusivity is a machine fact about this position.

Rxa8 is illegal because the defending king stands on e8 between the rooks — square arithmetic, checkable from the FEN. The passive rook did not just lose time; it chose the one square its own king disconnects.

This root is the position one move after the defence drill philidor-third-rank-hold plays 1...Rh8?? — the deviation that pack queries as a loss. Held fence: draw; passive rook: this pack. The two packs are the same family seen from both benches.

Outcome drill: after the skewer you are graded on converting, not on matching the authored squares. The tablebase confirms several escorts; king-before-pawn is the one that generalizes across the family.
